analysis.one_liner: Sets federal privacy rules for companies that collect and sell personal data and expands protections for kids online.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created the first broad federal framework for how companies collect, use, and sell personal information. It would have required companies to secure the data they hold, tell people what they collect and get opt-in consent before using it for behavioral advertising, collect only what they need, and notify people and law enforcement after a breach. A separate title, the Do Not Track Kids Act, would have restricted targeted advertising to children and teens and given parents tools to delete a child's data. The FTC, state attorneys general, and the Justice Department would enforce the rules. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose personal data is gathered, combined, and sold online, and especially children and teens who are tracked for advertising. Anyone whose information was exposed in a breach would have gained rights to prompt notice and free credit reports.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to take security measures proportionate to the data they hold, to follow privacy-by-design practices, and to give people clear notice of what is collected and why [S3].
Requires opt-in consent before a company uses personal information in ways people did not authorize, and before third parties use it for behavioral advertising [S3].
Limits collection and retention to what is reasonably necessary to deliver a service, and restricts transfers to third parties [S2] [S3].
Requires prompt breach notification to individuals and law enforcement, plus free credit reports for two years for people notified of a breach [S3].

Restricts targeted marketing to children, extends protections to teens under the Do Not Track Kids Act title, and creates an eraser button so parents and minors can remove content and personal information [S2] [S3].
Gives the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general authority to enforce the rules with civil penalties [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect and sell personal data — data brokers, ad-tech firms, and online platforms — would bear compliance costs, lose access to unconstrained data trading, and face civil penalties for violations. Smaller firms would get scaled-down requirements and possible waivers.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives individuals no private right of action — people could not sue companies that misuse their data; only the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general could act [S3].
It preempts state privacy laws covering the same ground, replacing potentially stronger state rules with the federal floor [S3].

Penalties are capped: the Attorney General is limited to $3 million per breach (doubled for reckless or repeated violations), and state-enforcement penalties top out at $6 million per related series of violations [S3].

Companies can win exemption from the consent and data-minimization requirements by joining an industry-administered 'safe harbor' program that the FTC merely supervises, and the bill directs the Commerce Department to work with industry to develop codes of conduct — leaving much of the policing to private organizations [S3].
The rules apply only to entities handling data on more than 5,000 people, and small businesses can obtain waivers or modified breach-notification duties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given Americans something they currently lack: a national baseline of rights over their own data, with real enforcement. Its design weakens that promise — no right to sue, capped penalties, broad exemptions for small firms, and industry-run safe harbors that could let companies self-certify compliance — and preemption would lock in that floor over stronger state laws. Even so, the consumer protections are substantial, and the children's title addresses marketing practices that currently face little regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Albio Sires introduced the bill on December 4, 2017 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on December 4, 2017, and to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection on December 8, 2017 [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and platforms that profit from collecting and selling personal information kept operating under the existing patchwork of industry self-regulation and state laws, with no federal baseline of consumer rights.

for.name: Rep. Albio Sires
for.what_they_did: Introduced the commercial privacy and children's online privacy bill and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or a floor vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member signed on, so the partisan split was never tested; a Democrat sponsored the bill in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: Had it passed, the bill would have required opt-in consent for behavioral advertising, limited what data they could collect and sell, and exposed them to penalties. These firms profit from tracking people without those limits, so their business interest ran against the consumers the bill protected.

industries.industry: Online platforms and websites collecting user data
industries.note: They would face compliance costs and consent requirements for ad targeting, but the bill also left broad exceptions for first-party marketing, internal operations, and site analytics, and allowed industry-run safe harbor programs to substitute for direct compliance.

The bill would have let FTC-approved nongovernmental organizations run 'safe harbor' programs that exempt member companies from key consent and data-minimization rules, making private industry bodies permanent co-regulators of privacy — a role that would have been locked in even as the bill regulated the data trade.
